text: Entanglement gets described with a lot of mystical language — spooky action, instant correlation across any distance. Underneath all of that, it has an exact, checkable mathematical definition, built directly from the tensor product: an entangled state is simply a vector that cannot be written as a tensor product of two smaller vectors.

A 2-qubit state is a product state if it can be written as one qubit's own state tensored with the other qubit's own state. Expanding that out always gives the pattern a c, a d, b c, b d for some numbers a, b, c, d — the amplitudes factor into an 'a,b part' times a 'c,d part.' A state that provably cannot fit that pattern is called entangled.

One of the most important 2-qubit states in quantum computing is the Bell state, ket-zero-zero plus ket-one-one, over the square root of 2 — as a vector, that's 1 over root 2, 0, 0, 1 over root 2. It's correctly normalized, and nothing about the vector itself looks unusual.

Does it fit the product-state pattern for some a, b, c, d? Matching entry by entry, the second equation forces either a or d to be zero. If a is zero, the first equation breaks, since it needs a nonzero result. If d is zero, the fourth equation breaks the same way. Every path leads to a contradiction — there's no choice of a, b, c, d, real or complex, that reproduces this vector as a tensor product.

That unsolvability is the entire definition of entanglement — there's no way to describe qubit 1 on its own and qubit 2 on its own and have their tensor product reproduce this vector. The tell-tale sign is nonzero amplitudes on the matching outcomes and exactly zero on the mismatched ones. And the proof never once mentions distance, time, or signaling — entanglement is a pure property of the mathematical state.
